items.content:
RT @andriinb: An enterprise environment emits billions of log events every day. During an incident, the responder rarely needs all of them. They need the few hundred or thousands that tell the story: the burst of 4625 failures followed by a single 4624 success, the encoded PowerShell spawned by winword.exe, the new service installed at 03:12 on a domain controller. Logs analysis is the discipline of getting from the first number to the second fast enough to matter.

That job has become harder in two directions at once. Attackers using AI tooling generate evidence at machine speed and pad real actions with benign-looking activity. Meanwhile, the obvious shortcut of pushing logs into an LLM runs into guardrails, context-window limits and data-protection obligations. Hugging Face’s responders hit exactly that wall in July 2026, when roughly 17,000 , later to be claimed 3 billion events (still healthy daily workload) were refused by frontier models and had to be processed on a local model instead.

Below, we cover log analysis end to end, then look at LogTotal, SOC Prime’s free answer to the incident-time version of the problem. https://t.co/wZaxcJwecZ

What it covers:

[+] The bug: a heap overflow (CWE-122) in the Print Spooler's form-enumeration path, reached
through InternalEnumForms → CopyIniFormToFormInfo → PackStrings → memcpy. 

[+] It is still unpatched. I submitted it to Microsoft in March 2026 and MSRC assessed it as below the bar for
immediate servicing, because the PoC requires administrative rights. Re-confirmed working in October against current mainstream and Canary builds.

[+] The exploitation, which is two thirds of the article, with four stages: groom, corrupt, control, execute. The process never crashes: spoolsv.exe is left running and the planted form deleted. 

[+] Important note: I had already notified the MSRC months ago that I would write an article about the vulnerability and publish it.

I would like to thank Ilfak Guilfanov ( @ilfak ) and Hex-Rays SA ( @HexRaysSA ) for the continuous

items.content:
My concern with the upcoming PHP RCE disclosure is how many systems could remain exposed long after patches become available.

Roughly a third of PHP websites still run PHP 5 or 7. Some operators will need to migrate old applications before they can move to a supported release. Even on supported versions, plenty of systems won't be patched immediately. Some owners won't notice the advisory; others can't deploy an update that quickly.

We still need the technical details to understand the actual exposure. If reliable, unauthenticated exploitation works across common deployments, I'd expect automated mass exploitation very quickly. AI-assisted exploit development and payload adaptation could shorten the response window further.

For detection teams, I'd prepare now for the activity that follows. I expect plenty of familiar shells, downloaders, webshells and persistence mechanisms, even though the entry point is new.

I've published a process-watcher guide with PHP configurations to record descendant processes and their command lines, with optional termination rules for shells, interpreters and known payload patterns:

https://t.co/7nluFV3Q25

Short-lived commands can still be recorded, even when they finish before the kill response arrives. Activity entirely inside the PHP worker remains a blind spot.

THOR Lite already includes relevant detections. We'll also review internally what additional post-exploitation coverage we can make publicly available.

After patching, check for compromise. An update doesn't remove an existing webshell or invalidate stolen credentials.

RT @joshua_saxe: The big surprise of the 2022–26 era for AI security policy is how cyber damages to the public don't seem to have increased much due to AI. In fact, they've stayed on-trend with the industrialization-of-cybercrime growth rates we've observed since around 2015, with perhaps a small AI-causal bump.

It's useful to think about the position of cybercriminals to develop an intuition for this:
* Imagine you're trying to build a cybercrime business and you want to take advantage of AI automation.
* How do you find and retain talented engineers who can build and operate the software/infra stack you'll need, given that they'll often have non-criminal alternatives with today's AI labor demand (even in middle-income countries where this demand also exists)?
* Where are you going to rent space for your workforce to work?
* Who are you going to hire who's willing to live there and live a life of crime?
* If you're running your business remotely, how will you ensure honor among thieves and manage hiring and firing?
* What's your strategy for evading law enforcement and bribing your way out of trouble?
* How can you access AI inference in a stable way that allows you to innovate your work processes and tech stack?
* Given all this, how will your quarterly automation goals compare to those of, say, a regional call center business in the American Midwest?
There's a lot of nuance here (e.g., state and state-sponsored cyber attackers are a very different group; capabilities can get built up there and then unleashed discontinuously, and this needs to be considered).
But overall, the demographic picture of cyber attackers means that folks should stop thinking of cyber attackers as a bunch of implicit MIT grads anxious to absorb the latest in automation to scale their businesses...

Assumptions are at the root of so many security issues. When testing an application or reviewing code, always ask yourself: "What assumptions did the developer make? What assumptions am I making when I say this is secure?"

Maybe you're assuming that an input has already been validated, that a route requires authentication, or that a framework handles a security check for you. 

Each of those assumptions deserves to be verified.

Questioning the developer's assumptions is part of the job, but questioning your own is just as important.

items.content:
RT @snggle_: Was iPhone security broken just with Bluetooth?

iPhone was always known for its high security, second only to GrapheneOS. But a leaked Cellebrite document might show they found a way to break their protection.

The device is more vulnerable in AFU (After First Unlock) than in BFU (Before First Unlock). 
Cellebrite's "Advanced Unlock" allegedly has the capability to unlock devices in the AFU state. As a response to rising USB port protection, they answered with a method capable of bypassing encryption over the Bluetooth radio.

No pairing, no user interaction. The Bluetooth attack sends an L2CAP packet to the target that hijacks the Bluetooth daemon and gains kernel-level control.

What is interesting is that Apple patched this with the iPhone 17 and TOLD NO ONE. They implemented MIE (Memory Integrity Enforcement), which might also be proof that these alleged capabilities are real, and that devices older than the iPhone 17 are vulnerable to these attacks.

GrapheneOS documentation states that this attack vector is known and won't work on up-to-date GrapheneOS devices.

GrapheneOS will always be the safest option.
